front: What is a fluid, and how does it differ from a solid in resisting shear?
back: A fluid is any substance that can flow (liquids and gases). Unlike solids, fluids have no definite shape; gases fill their container; and the shearing stress of a fluid is about a million times smaller than that of a solid — a fluid deforms continuously under shear.

front: Define pressure, give its unit/dimension, and explain why a fluid at rest exerts only normal forces.
back: Pressure P = F/A (the normal force per unit area); SI unit pascal (Pa) = N m⁻²; dimension [ML⁻¹T⁻²]; 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. Tangential forces would set the fluid flowing, impossible at rest — so forces on any surface are strictly normal.

front: State Pascal's law in both its forms.
back: (1) In a fluid at rest the pressure is the same at all points on a given horizontal plane. (2) External pressure applied on any part of a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished and equally in all directions — the basis of hydraulic machines and brakes.

front: Derive the pressure at depth h and state the hydrostatic paradox.
back: Equilibrating a vertical liquid column of base A and height h: (P₂ − P₁)A = ρhAg ⟹ P₂ − P₁ = ρgh, and open to air P = P_atm + ρgh. Hydrostatic paradox: bottom pressure depends only on height (and ρ), not on vessel shape or liquid quantity.

front: How does a mercury barometer measure atmospheric pressure, and what are torr and bar?
back: A mercury-filled tube inverted in a trough holds a column whose weight balances P_atm: P_a = ρ_Hg·g·h, h ≈ 76 cm = 1 atm at sea level. 1 torr = 1 mm of Hg = 133 Pa; 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa (meteorology uses millibars).

front: How do hydraulic lift and hydraulic brakes exploit Pascal's law, and what is the price paid?
back: P = F₁/A₁ is transmitted undiminished, so F₂ = (A₂/A₁)F₁ — mechanical advantage A₂/A₁ (lift; equal braking effort at all four wheels). Price: the large piston's displacement is shorter in the ratio A₁/A₂ (incompressible volume conservation).

front: Define streamline flow and write the equation of continuity.
back: Steady flow: velocity at each point is time-independent. A streamline is a curve whose tangent everywhere gives the fluid velocity; no two streamlines cross. Continuity (mass conservation for incompressible flow): Av = constant, so the fluid speeds up in constrictions.

front: State and derive Bernoulli's equation.
back: From work-energy: net work (P₁ − P₂)ΔV = ΔK + ΔU = ½ρΔV(v₂² − v₁²) + ρgΔV(h₂ − h₁) ⟹ P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂. Valid for steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow; reduces to hydrostatics when v = 0.

front: Drive Torricelli's law for efflux from a tank open to the atmosphere.
back: Bernoulli between the surface (v ≈ 0, P = P_atm) and the hole (P = P_atm): ½ρv² = ρg(y₂ − y₁) ⟹ v = √(2gh) — the free-fall speed. In a pressure vessel the entry P − P_a enters too: v² = 2gh + 2(P − P_a)/ρ.

front: Explain dynamic lift for a spinning ball (Magnus effect) and an aerofoil.
back: The body disturbs/rotates the airflow, making the air speed higher on one side; Bernoulli then gives lower pressure on that side and a sideways/upward force. An aerofoil crowds streamlines on top (faster air, lower pressure) ⟹ lift. Speed difference of only ~8% over a 500 m² wing lifts a 3.3 × 10⁵ kg aircraft.

front: Define viscosity, its unit, and how it varies with temperature for liquids vs gases.
back: Viscosity is internal friction opposing the relative motion of fluid layers: η = (F/A)/(v/l) = shearing stress/strain rate (SI: poiseuille Pl = Pa s). Liquids: η falls as temperature rises; gases: η rises (faster random molecular transport).

front: What determines terminal velocity? Give Stokes' law and the formula.
back: Stokes' drag F = 6πηav balances buoyancy plus weight at terminal speed: 6πηav_t = (4/3)πa³(ρ − σ)g ⟹ v_t = 2a²(ρ − σ)g/(9η). v_t grows as the square of the radius, so fine dust or tiny raindrops fall extremely slowly.

front: Why do surface molecules have extra energy, and what consequence does that have for a liquid?
back: An interior molecule is attracted on all sides (large negative potential energy); a surface molecule is pulled only from its lower side, keeping roughly half the cohesion energy. A liquid thus seeks the least surface area for its volume — droplets are spherical (the minimum-area shape).

front: How is surface tension defined both as force and as energy? Derive S = F/2l.
back: Surface tension S = surface energy per unit area = force per unit length. A bar of length l sliding distance d on a film creates area 2ld (two surfaces); work Fd = S(2ld) ⟹ S = F/2l. Water at 20 °C: 0.073 N/m; falls with temperature.

front: Define angle of contact and write the interfacial-tension equilibrium.
back: θ is the angle between the liquid-surface tangent at the contact line and the solid surface (measured inside the liquid). Equilibrium: S_la cosθ + S_sl = S_sa. S_sl > S_la ⟹ obtuse θ, no wetting (mercury/glass, water on wax); S_sl < S_la ⟹ acute θ, wetting (water on glass/plastic, detergents).

front: Give the excess pressure inside a drop, a soap bubble, and an air bubble in a liquid.
back: Spherical drop: P_i − P_o = 2S/r. Soap bubble (two surfaces): P_i − P_o = 4S/r. Air bubble inside a liquid (one surface): P_i − P_o = 2S/r. The convex side of a liquid–gas interface always carries the higher pressure.

front: Derive the capillary rise and explain why mercury is depressed.
back: Pressure just below a concave meniscus is P_atm − 2S cosθ/a; equating to the hydrostatic column: ρgh = 2S cosθ/a ⟹ h = 2S cosθ/(ρga). Water in a 0.05 cm capillary: ~3 cm. Mercury has cosθ < 0, so its column is depressed below the outer level.

front: Recreate Example 9.7: lift and fractional speed change of a Boeing 747.
back: (a) Level flight: ΔP × A = mg ⟹ ΔP = 3.3 × 10⁵ × 9.8/500 = 6.5 × 10³ Pa. (b) ΔP ≈ ρ v_av (v₂ − v₁), v_av = 267 m s⁻¹ ⟹ (v₂ − v₁)/v_av = 6.5 × 10³/(1.2 × 267²) ≈ 0.08 — only ~8% faster air on top needed.

front: Explain 9.6 (Pascal's wine barometer) and 9.7 (deep-oil-well structure suitability).
back: 9.6: h = P_atm/(ρg) = 1.013 × 10⁵/(984 × 9.8) = 10.5 m — a wine column — because wine is ~13.6/0.984 times less dense than mercury. 9.7: pressure at 3 km = ρgh ≈ 1.03 × 10³ × 9.8 × 3000 ≈ 3 × 10⁷ Pa < 10⁹ Pa limit ⟹ structure is suitable.

front: Explain why Bernoulli forbids using absolute vs gauge pressure, and why rapids are excluded.
back: Gauge pressure just subtracts the same atmospheric value from every term, which cancels in the equation — so results agree, provided the surrounding pressure is uniform. Rapids are excluded because Bernoulli requires steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow; rapids are turbulent and unsteady.

front: Explain Exercises 9.13 and 9.14 in outline.
Common traps in fluid-mechanics problems.
back: 1. Bernoulli assumes steady, ideal (non-viscous), incompressible flow — never apply to turbulence/rapids. 2. Soap bubble uses 4S/r, a drop or an air bubble in a liquid uses 2S/r. 3. Capillary: mercury is depressed (cosθ negative), water rises. 4. Pressure at depth ignores vessel shape/volume — only h, ρ, g. 5. Gauge pressure = P − P_atm; absolute vs gauge cancels in Bernoulli.
